title: Lena and the Winter
premise: Lena Vasseur, a property surveyor, arrives in the dying village of Saint-Aubin-du-Mont to appraise the Delacroix house for sale, only to find that her instruments record rooms that do not exist and a bell tower that was demolished in 1911. When the melted-down church bell rings at dusk, she is drawn into a founding ritual left unfinished by the village's ancestors, who bargained with something beneath the hill to survive their first winter. The founders' pact requires completion every hundred years, and the harvest moon is nine days away. To save herself and what remains of the village, Lena must finish the ritual the founders started—learning too late that its final step demands she surrender her memories of everyone she loves—and in the end she chooses to complete it anyway, trading her past for the village's future, waking on the first frost with no idea why the empty house feels like grief.
about_author: Lior Joubert is the pen name of a former land registry clerk from the Loire Valley who spent eleven years cataloguing deeds for houses that burned, collapsed, or simply stopped appearing on maps. Their fiction draws on the bureaucratic horror of paperwork that outlives the people it describes.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Lena. She arrives in Saint-Aubin-du-Mont to survey the Delacroix house, finding it immaculate though abandoned since 1974. Her laser measure returns impossible figures—one hallway eleven meters longer inside than out. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack into unease.

chapters.title: Rooms That Count Themselves
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Documenting everything as ritual, she sketches floor plans that redraw overnight, adding a room labeled in her own handwriting: 'the counting room.' The village's last resident, old Madame Perrin, warns her not to measure after dark. Beat: dread of complicity.

chapters.title: A Bell Melted in 1911
chapters.summary: POV Lena. In the parish archive she finds records of the bell sold and melted down for war metal in 1911, yet every villager's diary mentions hearing it ring each October. The tower's foundation stones are still warm. Beat: history refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: Silas Delacroix's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Lena. She discovers the surveyor Silas Delacroix's 1911 ledger in the cellar wall—his notes descend from measurements into prayers, then into instructions for 'finishing what we began.' The last page names a date: the harvest moon. Beat: awe curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: First Ringing
chapters.summary: POV Lena. At dusk the bell rings—a sound felt in teeth and ribs—and the village around her shifts; roads return to older shapes, and she sees lanterns moving in windows of houses long ruined. She is seen by something wearing a founder's coat. Beat: terror and terrible belonging.

chapters.title: Madame Perrin's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV alternating Lena/Madame Perrin. Perrin reveals her family has kept the vigil for generations, feeding the ritual small offerings so it stays dormant. This year the offering failed because the Delacroix house changed hands—changed hands to Lena. Beat: guilt and the weight of inheritance.

chapters.title: The Founders' Winter
chapters.summary: POV Lena, reading recovered journals. The 1712 founders, starving, made a covenant with the thing under the hill: memory given freely in exchange for survival. The bell was its voice until they tried to silence it. Beat: understanding that the village itself is the debt.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: POV Lena. The house begins rearranging to guide her—doors opening onto the counting room, where ledgers of every villager's surrendered memories line the shelves, hers already started, pages filling with childhood she doesn't remember giving. Beat: violation and vertigo.

chapters.title: Étienne
chapters.summary: POV Lena. A man appears claiming to be the estate's other appraiser—Étienne, warm, funny, impossible, since the firm sent no one. He knows the village's lost streets by heart. She falls for him even as she suspects he is the house speaking. Beat: love blooming in contaminated ground.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Perrin teaches her the ritual's structure from Delacroix's ledger: seven stations, six completed in 1911 before the founders' descendants fled. One night per station, ending at the harvest moon. Refusal means the thing beneath wakes unfed and unbound. Beat: duty closing like a trap.

chapters.title: Station of the Door
chapters.summary: POV Lena. First rite at the sunken chapel door: she must name aloud what she fears losing. The ground answers by showing her Étienne standing among the founders' portraits. Beat: the first cost made visible.

chapters.title: Station of the Well
chapters.summary: POV Lena. At the dry well she must surrender one true memory voluntarily. She gives up her mother's voice—and immediately cannot recall it, only that something is missing. Étienne comforts her; his hands are cold as well water. Beat: grief with no object.

chapters.title: The Village That Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Madame Perrin. Perrin's chapter: her childhood vigil, her sister taken by the hill in 1953, and her secret hope that this year someone will end it rather than feed it. She gives Lena her family's page of the covenant—the loophole clause. Beat: hope passed hand to hand.

chapters.title: Station of the Names
chapters.summary: POV Lena. In the ruined schoolhouse she must read the founders' names into the dark. Each name she speaks, she forgets a stranger less and a loved one more—the ritual takes by proximity. She falters at Étienne's name, which appears uninvited on the list. Beat: horror of the fine print.

chapters.title: What Étienne Is
chapters.summary: POV Lena. She confronts him; he admits he is the house's memory of Silas Delacroix's son, given shape to keep her willing. He begs her to stop the ritual and flee—but fleeing means the thing wakes, and he will be its mouth. Beat: love against duty, both losing.

chapters.title: Station of the Bell
chapters.summary: POV Lena. At the tower's foundation she rings the absent bell herself, striking the warm stone with the surveyor's hammer. The village below her hands becomes fully 1911 for one breath—crowds, lanterns, faces turning upward toward her. Beat: communion with the dead.

chapters.title: Perrin's Sacrifice
chapters.summary: POV alternating. Perrin attempts the seventh station alone to spare Lena, but the ritual rejects a unwilling gift and takes her entirely—her body found seated, smiling, empty. Lena finds the loophole clause clutched in Perrin's hand. Beat: devastating cost of good intentions.

chapters.title: The Loophole
chapters.summary: POV Lena. The clause: the covenant can be completed rather than renewed—if all seven stations are finished by one who gives memory knowingly and freely, the debt closes forever and the thing beneath sleeps without feeding. But 'all memory' means everything, including Étienne. Beat: resolve forged in loss.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: POV Lena. The moon rises fat and orange. The house unfolds its true geometry around her, corridors becoming the founders' original covenant path. Étienne walks beside her, begging her to forget him last so he can say goodbye. Beat: tenderness at the edge of annihilation.

chapters.title: The Seventh Station
chapters.summary: POV Lena, fragmenting. At the counting room she completes the ledger in her own blood-ink, surrendering each memory deliberately—mother, career, fear, and finally Étienne, who kisses her forehead and unravels mid-farewell. The bell rings once, whole and real. Beat: climax; sacrifice made luminous.

chapters.title: First Frost
chapters.summary: POV Lena. She wakes in the Delacroix house on a clean morning, her survey complete, her mind a smooth blank page. The village feels lighter; Perrin's grave bears fresh flowers from an unknown hand. On the last ledger page, in writing she doesn't recognize as hers: 'It is finished. Be happy.' Beat: hollow peace.

chapters.title: The House Remembers For You
chapters.summary: POV Lena, coda. Packing to leave, she finds a surveyor's notebook not in her handwriting—Silas's, or Étienne's, or hers—describing a woman who chose to forget so others could keep remembering. She pockets it, unable to explain why, and the bell does not ring. Beat: bittersweet resolution; memory outliving the rememberer.
